current_manifest_row_before.title: Both tails determine power for the known-variance two-sided normal z-test
current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be mutually independent with common law $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $n\ge1$ and $\sigma>0$. For the simple null $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ against the two-sided alternative $H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$, let $Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu_0)/\sigma$, let $c_\alpha=z_{1-\alpha/2}$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and reject when $|Z_n|>c_\alpha$. This test has size $\alpha$. At $\mu=\mu_0+\delta$, where $\delta\in\mathbb R$, its rejection probability (the power function evaluated at this parameter) is
$$1-\Phi(c_\alpha-\lambda)+\Phi(-c_\alpha-\lambda), \qquad \lambda=\frac{\sqrt n\,\delta}{\sigma}.$$
For $\delta\ne0$ this is power at the stated alternative; for $\delta=0$ it is the null rejection probability. The first term is the upper-tail rejection probability and the second is the lower-tail rejection probability.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.4, printed pp. 149–159
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, §7.2.2.2, PDF pp. 2019–2021

current_manifest_row_before.title: The backdoor criterion implies conditional exchangeability
current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on $G$. Let $T,W$ be disjoint
vertex sets and let $C$ be a set of nondescendants of $T$. Define the
response-family sigma-algebra
$$\mathcal R_W^T:=\sigma\{X_w^t:w\in W,\ t\in\prod_{v\in T}S_v\}.$$
If $C$ d-separates $T$ and $W$ in $G_{\underline T}$, then
$$\sigma(X_T)\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal R_W^T\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
For each fixed intervention value $t$, this implies
$X_W^t\perp\!\!\!\perp X_T\mid\sigma(X_C)$. No treatment-positivity
condition is needed.

current_manifest_row_before.title: Counterfactual identities under the front-door conditions
current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on a full DAG with observed
vertices $A,M,Y$ and any number of latent vertices. Suppose: (i) every
directed path from $A$ to $Y$ contains $M$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are
d-separated by the empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$
d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline M}$. For each supplied value
$a\in S_A$, let $M^a$ be the response under $do(A=a)$. Define
$$I_M=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline A}}(M)\setminus\{A\},\qquad I_Y=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline M}}(Y)\setminus\{M\},$$
where ancestry includes the vertex itself and $U_I$ is the finite vector of
exogenous coordinates $(U_v)_{v\in I}$. Then $M^a$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_M})$, each response $Y^m$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_Y})$, and
$$M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A,\qquad I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing,\qquad M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y},\qquad M\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A.$$
The recursive responses also satisfy $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$ almost surely. The
conditional independence is for the factual law; it supplies a genuine
conditional product law for the exogenous coordinates used by the outcome
response.

Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Point 7.4, p. 101

current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM on a finite DAG $G$. Let $A$ be an
observed countable-valued treatment, $Y$ an observed standard-Borel outcome,
and $L$ an observed finite vector of standard-Borel vertices containing no
descendant of $A$. Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose (i) $L$
d-separates $A$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline A}$ and (ii) a regular conditional
propensity $e_a(L)=P(A=a\mid L)$ is strictly positive $P_L$-almost surely.
Then for every Borel set $B$ in the state space of $Y$,
$$P(Y^a\in B)=\int P(Y\in B\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
The right side depends only on the observed law. Thus the law of $Y^a$ is an
identifiable estimand on any statistical model consisting of such SCMs with
the same observed variables. If $Y$ is real and $Y^a$ is integrable, applying
the identity to bounded truncations and taking limits gives
$$E[Y^a]=\int E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
For a continuous treatment, the corresponding regular conditional formula is
identified only for $P_A$-almost every $a$; this theorem makes no pointwise
claim at a null treatment value.

current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM with observed countable-valued
treatment $A$, observed standard-Borel mediator $M$, and real outcome $Y$.
Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose in the full DAG: (i) $M$ lies on
every directed path from $A$ to $Y$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are d-separated by the
empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$ d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in
$G_{\underline M}$. Write $\mu_a=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a)$ and, for every
positive-probability treatment atom $a'$, write
$\mu_{a'}=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a')$. Assume the nested-law support condition
$$\mu_a\ll\mu_{a'}\qquad\text{for every }a'\text{ with }P(A=a')>0,$$
and absolute integrability of the nested conditional means:
$$\int\!\int E(|Y|\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da')\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty.$$
Then
$$E[Y^a]=\int P(dm\mid A=a)\int E(Y\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da').$$
The right side is determined by the observed law, so the interventional mean
is identifiable on any statistical model of SCMs satisfying these
assumptions. For a discrete mediator, the support condition says that every
mediator value having positive probability under $A=a$ also has positive
probability under every positive-probability treatment atom. These are
sufficient conditions only. For non-atomic treatment values, regular
conditional formulas are determined only $P_A$-almost everywhere; this
item makes no pointwise claim at a null treatment value.

Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$ and $Y^a\in L^1(P)$. Assume consistency $Y=Y^A$, conditional exchangeability $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity $e_a(L):=P(A=a\mid\sigma(L))>0$ almost surely. For $I_a=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}$ and the observed law $Q$ of $(A,L,Y)$, the inverse-probability-weighted functional of [[alg-inverse-probability-weighting-for-a-causal-mean]] is well-defined and satisfies
$$E_Q\!\left[\frac{I_aY}{e_a(L)}\right]=E_P[Y^a].$$
Consequently, it identifies the population mean of $Y^a$ in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]. No uniform lower bound on $e_a$ is assumed. This is a population identity for the true propensity, not a finite-sample stability or estimated-weight result.

consistency use [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]; conditional
exchangeability is the full-family sigma-algebra condition of
[[def-conditional-exchangeability-of-potential-outcomes]]. More generally,
for a treatment in any measurable space with measurable singleton $\{a\}$,

conditionally independent of $A$ given $\sigma(L)$ and

a global measurable selection $Y^A$ outside the target atom.

current_manifest_row_before.title: Conditional-class standardization identifies a causal mean

proposed_manifest_row_after.title: Conditional-class standardization identifies a causal mean
proposed_manifest_row_after.statement:
Assume AC for the conditional-expectation existence convention. Consider a full-data law $P$ with an observed discrete or atomic treatment $A$, covariate random element $L$, observed outcome $Y$, and potential outcomes $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}$, with supplied potential outcomes (the countably discrete convention is [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]). Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$ and $Y^a\in L^1(P)$. Assume consistency $Y=Y^A$, conditional exchangeability $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity
$$e_a(L):=P(A=a\mid\sigma(L))>0\quad P\text{-almost surely}.$$
Let $Q$ be the observed-data law of $(A,L,Y)$, put $\mathcal G=\sigma(L)$ and $I_a=\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}$, and define the standardization functional $\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)$ as in [[alg-standardization-for-a-causal-mean]]. Then
$$\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)=E_P[Y^a].$$
Thus the observed law and the stated causal assumptions identify the population mean of $Y^a$, in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]. No lower bound $e_a(L)\ge\varepsilon>0$ is needed. This result is for a fixed atomic treatment value; it makes no pointwise claim for a continuous treatment.

For countably discrete treatments, the supplied potential outcomes and global
consistency use [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]; conditional
exchangeability is the full-family sigma-algebra condition of
[[def-conditional-exchangeability-of-potential-outcomes]]. More generally,
for a treatment in any measurable space with measurable singleton $\{a\}$,
the same conclusion holds whenever the supplied integrable $Y^a$ is
conditionally independent of $A$ given $\sigma(L)$ and
$\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a$ almost surely, with the same
positive propensity. This atom-consistency formulation does not require
a global measurable selection $Y^A$ outside the target atom.

domain of [[thm-discrete-treatment-potential-outcome-mean-identification]],
this conditional-class functional equals that theorem's RCD standardization
functional. The application here also allows arbitrary covariate random
elements and uses the algorithm's version-free conditional class.

proposed_manifest_row_after.title: The continuous survival and cumulative-hazard identity
proposed_manifest_row_after.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T$ be a nonnegative event
time with a finite-valued density $f$ relative to Lebesgue measure, so
$P_T(A)=\int_A f(u)\,du$ for every Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and assume
$S_T(0)=1$. Let
$$\tau_*:=\inf\{t\ge0:S_T(t)=0\},$$
with $\tau_*=+\infty$ if this set is empty. For every $0\le t<\tau_*$,
$$S_T(t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_0^t\frac{f(u)}{S_T(u)}\,du\right).$$
If $\tau_*<\infty$, the improper cumulative hazard tends to $+\infty$ as
$t\uparrow\tau_*$; extending it by $+\infty$ for $t\ge\tau_*$ gives the same
identity there with the convention $e^{-\infty}=0$. The density-hazard formula
is asserted only where $S_T>0$.

current_manifest_row_before.title: Right-censored exponential likelihood and its boundary maximum

proposed_manifest_row_after.title: Right-censored exponential likelihood and its boundary maximum
proposed_manifest_row_after.statement:
Assume Countable Choice.

Let $\lambda>0$ be an event-rate parameter and let $\psi\in\Psi$ index a
censoring-law family $G_\psi$ on $[0,\infty)$. For every $\psi$, assume
$G_\psi$ is a Borel probability measure with a specified finite-valued
Borel-measurable density $g_\psi$ relative to one fixed sigma-finite Borel
measure $\nu$ on $[0,\infty)$, where $\nu$ does not depend on $\lambda$ or
$\psi$.
Assume the parameter space is the product $(0,\infty)\times\Psi$: the event
law depends only on $\lambda$, the censor law only on $\psi$, and for each
subject $T_i\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ is independent of $C_i\sim G_\psi$.
The subject pairs are iid. Observe
$$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i),\qquad \delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\},$$
as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]. Write
$\bar G_\psi(u):=G_\psi([u,\infty))$.

On the one-subject observation space $[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}$ with the
product of the Borel sigma-algebra and the discrete sigma-algebra, let $\rho$
equal Lebesgue measure on the $\delta=1$ branch and $\nu$ on the $\delta=0$
branch; explicitly,
$$\rho(A)=\operatorname{Leb}\{u:(u,1)\in A\}+\nu\{u:(u,0)\in A\}$$
for measurable $A$. Then the observation law has the explicitly specified $\rho$-density
$$h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\bar G_\psi(u),\qquad h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,0)=e^{-\lambda u}g_\psi(u).$$
For $n\ge1$ subjects, set $d:=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_i$ and
$E:=\sum_{i=1}^n U_i$. For each fixed $(\lambda,\psi)$ and its displayed
density versions, the likelihood is, $\rho^{\otimes n}$-almost everywhere,
$$L(\lambda,\psi;\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta)=\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta),$$
where
$$C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta):=\prod_{i:\delta_i=1}\bar G_\psi(u_i)\prod_{i:\delta_i=0}g_\psi(u_i).$$
Thus, for fixed $\psi$ with $C_\psi>0$, the event-rate likelihood is
proportional to $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}$.

For such data: if $d>0$ and $E>0$, the unique maximum over $\lambda>0$ is
$\widehat\lambda=d/E$; if $d=0$ and $E>0$, the likelihood is strictly
decreasing, with supremum as $\lambda\downarrow0$ and no maximizer in
$(0,\infty)$. A formal likelihood extension to the boundary $\lambda=0$
attains that supremum there, but $\lambda=0$ is not a proper exponential law
for finite event times. If $d=0$ and $E=0$, the likelihood is constant in
$\lambda$. Under the model, $d>0,E=0$ occurs with probability zero. If
$C_\psi=0$, the likelihood version is zero for every $\lambda$ at that fixed
$\psi$, so the stated maximizing claims do not apply to that parameter value.

current_manifest_row_before.title: Method agreement and limits of agreement
current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be the declared probability model for a
pre-specified target population of measurement conditions. Let $A$ and $B$ be
real random variables giving quantitative measurements of the same target
under the same stated conditions. The choice of target population and the
scientific applicability of its probability law are model assumptions; this
definition does not verify them.

Assume the paired difference $D:=A-B$ is square-integrable. It is measurable
because measurable real functions are closed under finite sums and scalar
multiples ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).
Since $0\le(|D|-1)^2$, we have $|D|\le(D^2+1)/2$. Monotonicity,
homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral, together with
$\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$, give
$$\mathbb E[|D|]\le\tfrac12\mathbb E[D^2]+\tfrac12<\infty$$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). Thus define the finite
population bias $\mu_D:=\mathbb E[D]$. Put $H:=D-\mu_D$, which is measurable by
the same closure result. Its square $H^2$ is measurable by
[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Since
$$H^2\le 2D^2+2\mu_D^2,$$
monotonicity, homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral give
$$\mathbb E[H^2]\le 2\mathbb E[D^2]+2\mu_D^2<\infty$$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). Therefore
$$\sigma_D:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(D)}=\sqrt{\mathbb E[H^2]}$$
is a finite real standard deviation, since $\operatorname{Var}(D)=\mathbb E[H^2]$
by [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and every nonnegative real has a
square root by [[thm-of-square-roots]].
The sign convention is $D=A-B$, so positive bias means that $A$ reads larger
than $B$ on average. The conventional rounded normal-reference limits of
agreement are $\mu_D-1.96\sigma_D$ and $\mu_D+1.96\sigma_D$.

For an iid sample $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ of paired differences from the declared
target population, with $n\ge2$ and observed values $d_1,\ldots,d_n$, define
$$\bar d:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i,\qquad s_D:=\sqrt{\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i-\bar d)^2}.$$
The sample plug-in limits are $\bar d\pm1.96s_D$: they substitute the sample
mean and sample standard deviation into the conventional population formula.
They are point estimates; no unbiasedness, consistency, confidence coverage,
or exact finite-sample coverage for either endpoint is asserted here.

Repeated measurements on one target are not iid merely because there are many
recorded pairs. Their within-target dependence must be stated and modeled, for
example with a covariance or random-effects model. When defined, correlation
measures linear association and does not by itself establish agreement. Limits
of agreement describe the distribution of differences; they do not decide
whether those differences are acceptable for a particular use or whether
either method is calibrated to a known truth.

current_manifest_row_before.title: A conditionally superuniform stage-2 p-value preserves conditional error
current_manifest_row_before.statement:
Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[thm-conditional-error-budget-two-stage-adaptation]], let $p_2$ be a
measurable stage-2 p-value with values in $[0,1]$. Choose an
$\mathcal F_1$-measurable representative $A$ of the original conditional-error
class that takes values in $[0,1]$ everywhere; such a representative exists by
clipping any version on its null exceptional set. Changing to this version
changes $R_2$ only on a null set. Suppose that for every
fixed $u\in[0,1]$,
$$E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le u\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le u\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
Then the adapted rejection event $R_2=\{p_2\le A\}$ satisfies
$$E_0[\mathbf1_{R_2}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le A\quad\text{almost surely},$$
and hence $P_0(R_2)\le\alpha$. The conditional p-value inequality is assumed
separately for each fixed $u$; no common exceptional set over all
$u\in[0,1]$ is required.
current_manifest_row_before.strategy:
**Proof technique:** approximate the interim-measurable threshold from above by finite-valued thresholds, then pass to the decreasing limit.

1.1 Conditional order and the constant rule [F5] give $0\le A\le1$ almost surely. Clipping a version on the measurable null set where it leaves $[0,1]$ preserves its conditional-expectation class and changes $R_2$ only on a null set, so take $0\le A\le1$ everywhere. For each integer $n\ge1$, define $A_n=2^{-n}\lceil2^nA\rceil$. Its level sets are $\{A_n=0\}=\{A=0\}$ and $\{A_n=k2^{-n}\}=\{(k-1)2^{-n}<A\le k2^{-n}\}$ for $1\le k\le2^n$, so they are in $\mathcal F_1$. The inequality $\lceil2x\rceil\le2\lceil x\rceil$ shows $A_{n+1}\le A_n$, and $0\le A_n-A<2^{-n}$, hence $A_n$ is finite-valued and $A_n\downarrow A$. Write its values as $t_{n,k}=k2^{-n}$, $k=0,\ldots,2^n$, and put $S_{n,k}=\{A_n=t_{n,k}\}$. By [F2], the events $\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}$ are measurable. Let $Q_n=E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le A_n\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]$. The disjoint partition by $S_{n,k}$, linearity [F5], and taking out the bounded known indicator [F3] give $Q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}t_{n,k}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}=A_n$ almost surely. For all $n$ these inequalities hold on one probability-one set, because only countably many fixed dyadic thresholds occur. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 The events $B_n=\{p_2\le A_n\}$ decrease to $B=\{p_2\le A\}$. Their complement indicators are bounded and hence integrable, and increase to $\mathbf1_{B^c}$. Thus [F4] gives $E_0[\mathbf1_{B_n^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]\uparrow E_0[\mathbf1_{B^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]$ almost surely. By linearity and the constant rule [F5], this is equivalent to $Q_n\downarrow Q:=E_0[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_1]$. Taking limits in step 1.1 and using $A_n\downarrow A$ yields $Q\le A$ almost surely. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F6] to $R_2=B$: its conditional rejection probability is the $Q$ of step 2.1 and is at most $A$, while the original conditional-error budget has expectation at most $\alpha$. Therefore $P_0(R_2)\le\alpha$. [F6, step 2.1] ∎

patch.before: The claim that OLS is BLUE for every mean-zero error law with finite second moments under a full-rank fixed design, regardless of error covariance, is false.
patch.after:
For every full-column-rank fixed design and every mean-zero error law with
finite second moments, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator of every
contrast, regardless of the error covariance.

Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on a full DAG with observed
vertices $A,M,Y$ and any number of latent vertices. Suppose: (i) every
directed path from $A$ to $Y$ contains $M$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are
d-separated by the empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$
d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline M}$. For each supplied value
$a\in S_A$, let $M^a$ be the response under $do(A=a)$. Define
$$I_M=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline A}}(M)\setminus\{A\},\qquad I_Y=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline M}}(Y)\setminus\{M\},$$
where ancestry includes the vertex itself and $U_I$ is the finite vector of
exogenous coordinates $(U_v)_{v\in I}$. Then $M^a$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_M})$, each response $Y^m$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_Y})$, and
$$M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A,\qquad I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing,\qquad M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y},\qquad M\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A.$$
The recursive responses also satisfy $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$ almost surely. The
conditional independence is for the factual law; it supplies a genuine
conditional product law for the exogenous coordinates used by the outcome
response.

Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM on a finite DAG $G$. Let $A$ be an
observed countable-valued treatment, $Y$ an observed standard-Borel outcome,
and $L$ an observed finite vector of standard-Borel vertices containing no
descendant of $A$. Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose (i) $L$
d-separates $A$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline A}$ and (ii) a regular conditional
propensity $e_a(L)=P(A=a\mid L)$ is strictly positive $P_L$-almost surely.
Then for every Borel set $B$ in the state space of $Y$,
$$P(Y^a\in B)=\int P(Y\in B\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
The right side depends only on the observed law. Thus the law of $Y^a$ is an
identifiable estimand on any statistical model consisting of such SCMs with
the same observed variables. If $Y$ is real and $Y^a$ is integrable, applying
the identity to bounded truncations and taking limits gives
$$E[Y^a]=\int E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
For a continuous treatment, the corresponding regular conditional formula is
identified only for $P_A$-almost every $a$; this theorem makes no pointwise
claim at a null treatment value.

Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM with observed countable-valued
treatment $A$, observed standard-Borel mediator $M$, and real outcome $Y$.
Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose in the full DAG: (i) $M$ lies on
every directed path from $A$ to $Y$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are d-separated by the
empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$ d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in
$G_{\underline M}$. Write $\mu_a=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a)$ and, for every
positive-probability treatment atom $a'$, write
$\mu_{a'}=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a')$. Assume the nested-law support condition
$$\mu_a\ll\mu_{a'}\qquad\text{for every }a'\text{ with }P(A=a')>0,$$
and absolute integrability of the nested conditional means:
$$\int\!\int E(|Y|\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da')\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty.$$
Then
$$E[Y^a]=\int P(dm\mid A=a)\int E(Y\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da').$$
The right side is determined by the observed law, so the interventional mean
is identifiable on any statistical model of SCMs satisfying these
assumptions. For a discrete mediator, the support condition says that every
mediator value having positive probability under $A=a$ also has positive
probability under every positive-probability treatment atom. These are
sufficient conditions only. For non-atomic treatment values, regular
conditional formulas are determined only $P_A$-almost everywhere; this
item makes no pointwise claim at a null treatment value.

Assume AC for the conditional-expectation existence convention. Let $P$ be a full-data law with a discrete or atomic treatment $A$, covariate random element $L$, observed outcome $Y$, and potential outcomes $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}$ with the countably discrete convention given by [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$ and $Y^a\in L^1(P)$. Assume consistency $Y=Y^A$, conditional exchangeability $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity $e_a(L):=P(A=a\mid\sigma(L))>0$ almost surely. For $I_a=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}$ and the observed law $Q$ of $(A,L,Y)$, the inverse-probability-weighted functional of [[alg-inverse-probability-weighting-for-a-causal-mean]] is well-defined and satisfies
$$E_Q\!\left[\frac{I_aY}{e_a(L)}\right]=E_P[Y^a].$$
Consequently, it identifies the population mean of $Y^a$ in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]. No uniform lower bound on $e_a$ is assumed. This is a population identity for the true propensity, not a finite-sample stability or estimated-weight result.

For countably discrete treatments, the supplied potential outcomes and global
consistency use [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]; conditional
exchangeability is the full-family sigma-algebra condition of
[[def-conditional-exchangeability-of-potential-outcomes]]. More generally,
for a treatment in any measurable space with measurable singleton $\{a\}$,
the same conclusion holds whenever the supplied integrable $Y^a$ is
conditionally independent of $A$ given $\sigma(L)$ and
$\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a$ almost surely, with the same
positive propensity. This atom-consistency formulation does not require
a global measurable selection $Y^A$ outside the target atom.

Assume AC for the conditional-expectation existence convention. Consider a full-data law $P$ with an observed discrete or atomic treatment $A$, covariate random element $L$, observed outcome $Y$, and potential outcomes $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}$, with supplied potential outcomes (the countably discrete convention is [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]). Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$ and $Y^a\in L^1(P)$. Assume consistency $Y=Y^A$, conditional exchangeability $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity
$$e_a(L):=P(A=a\mid\sigma(L))>0\quad P\text{-almost surely}.$$
Let $Q$ be the observed-data law of $(A,L,Y)$, put $\mathcal G=\sigma(L)$ and $I_a=\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}$, and define the standardization functional $\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)$ as in [[alg-standardization-for-a-causal-mean]]. Then
$$\Psi_{\mathrm{std}}(Q;a)=E_P[Y^a].$$
Thus the observed law and the stated causal assumptions identify the population mean of $Y^a$, in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]. No lower bound $e_a(L)\ge\varepsilon>0$ is needed. This result is for a fixed atomic treatment value; it makes no pointwise claim for a continuous treatment.

For countably discrete treatments, the supplied potential outcomes and global
consistency use [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]; conditional
exchangeability is the full-family sigma-algebra condition of
[[def-conditional-exchangeability-of-potential-outcomes]]. More generally,
for a treatment in any measurable space with measurable singleton $\{a\}$,
the same conclusion holds whenever the supplied integrable $Y^a$ is
conditionally independent of $A$ given $\sigma(L)$ and
$\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y=\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a$ almost surely, with the same
positive propensity. This atom-consistency formulation does not require
a global measurable selection $Y^A$ outside the target atom.

On the overlapping countably discrete treatment and standard-Borel covariate
domain of [[thm-discrete-treatment-potential-outcome-mean-identification]],
this conditional-class functional equals that theorem's RCD standardization
functional. The application here also allows arbitrary covariate random
elements and uses the algorithm's version-free conditional class.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T$ be a nonnegative event
time with a finite-valued density $f$ relative to Lebesgue measure, so
$P_T(A)=\int_A f(u)\,du$ for every Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and assume
$S_T(0)=1$. Let
$$\tau_*:=\inf\{t\ge0:S_T(t)=0\},$$
with $\tau_*=+\infty$ if this set is empty. For every $0\le t<\tau_*$,
$$S_T(t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_0^t\frac{f(u)}{S_T(u)}\,du\right).$$
If $\tau_*<\infty$, the improper cumulative hazard tends to $+\infty$ as
$t\uparrow\tau_*$; extending it by $+\infty$ for $t\ge\tau_*$ gives the same
identity there with the convention $e^{-\infty}=0$. The density-hazard formula
is asserted only where $S_T>0$.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $\lambda>0$ be an event-rate parameter and let $\psi\in\Psi$ index a
censoring-law family $G_\psi$ on $[0,\infty)$. For every $\psi$, assume
$G_\psi$ is a Borel probability measure with a specified finite-valued
Borel-measurable density $g_\psi$ relative to one fixed sigma-finite Borel
measure $\nu$ on $[0,\infty)$, where $\nu$ does not depend on $\lambda$ or
$\psi$.
Assume the parameter space is the product $(0,\infty)\times\Psi$: the event
law depends only on $\lambda$, the censor law only on $\psi$, and for each
subject $T_i\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ is independent of $C_i\sim G_\psi$.
The subject pairs are iid. Observe
$$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i),\qquad \delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\},$$
as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]. Write
$\bar G_\psi(u):=G_\psi([u,\infty))$.

On the one-subject observation space $[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}$ with the
product of the Borel sigma-algebra and the discrete sigma-algebra, let $\rho$
equal Lebesgue measure on the $\delta=1$ branch and $\nu$ on the $\delta=0$
branch; explicitly,
$$\rho(A)=\operatorname{Leb}\{u:(u,1)\in A\}+\nu\{u:(u,0)\in A\}$$
for measurable $A$. Then the observation law has the explicitly specified $\rho$-density
$$h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\bar G_\psi(u),\qquad h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,0)=e^{-\lambda u}g_\psi(u).$$
For $n\ge1$ subjects, set $d:=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_i$ and
$E:=\sum_{i=1}^n U_i$. For each fixed $(\lambda,\psi)$ and its displayed
density versions, the likelihood is, $\rho^{\otimes n}$-almost everywhere,
$$L(\lambda,\psi;\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta)=\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta),$$
where
$$C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta):=\prod_{i:\delta_i=1}\bar G_\psi(u_i)\prod_{i:\delta_i=0}g_\psi(u_i).$$
Thus, for fixed $\psi$ with $C_\psi>0$, the event-rate likelihood is
proportional to $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}$.

For such data: if $d>0$ and $E>0$, the unique maximum over $\lambda>0$ is
$\widehat\lambda=d/E$; if $d=0$ and $E>0$, the likelihood is strictly
decreasing, with supremum as $\lambda\downarrow0$ and no maximizer in
$(0,\infty)$. A formal likelihood extension to the boundary $\lambda=0$
attains that supremum there, but $\lambda=0$ is not a proper exponential law
for finite event times. If $d=0$ and $E=0$, the likelihood is constant in
$\lambda$. Under the model, $d>0,E=0$ occurs with probability zero. If
$C_\psi=0$, the likelihood version is zero for every $\lambda$ at that fixed
$\psi$, so the stated maximizing claims do not apply to that parameter value.

patch.before: For fixed sample size, cause count, and horizon, and any statistical experiment on the Borel space of observed records, the Aalen–Johansen survival and cumulative-incidence output vector is measurable and hence a statistic in that experiment; every event-time risk-set denominator is positive.
patch.after:
Fix $n\ge1$, finite $K$, and $t\ge0$, and let
$$\mathcal X=\big([0,\infty)\times\{0,1,\ldots,K\}\big)^n$$
carry its Borel sigma-algebra as a Euclidean subspace, where status $0$ denotes
censoring and status $k$ denotes an observed cause-$k$ event. Let $\mathsf E$
be any statistical experiment with sample space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal B(\mathcal X))$.
Equip
$\mathbb R^{K+1}$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. The output vector of
[[alg-aalen-johansen-cumulative-incidence-estimator]] at horizon $t$ is a
measurable map $\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^{K+1}$ and hence a statistic in
$\mathsf E$. Every event-time denominator $Y(u)$ is positive.

patch.after:
Assume AC and $\sigma_0>0$. In the known-blank model
$X\sim N(c,\sigma_0^2)$, take
$\alpha=\beta=0.05$ and $k_Q=0.10$. Then
$$L_C=z_{0.95}\sigma_0,\qquad L_D=2z_{0.95}\sigma_0,\qquad L_Q=10\sigma_0.$$
The NIST SP 958 table reports the corresponding known-blank values rounded to
$1.64\sigma_0$, $3.29\sigma_0$, and $10\sigma_0$. These are conditional on
the equal-known-variance normal law and the stated error and CV targets.
